domain: International Law / Political Philosophy / Global Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the Treaty of Westphalia (1648) as a contested kernel establishing state sovereignty. Two competing readings: absolute sovereignty (non-interference principle) versus conditional sovereignty (responsibility to protect). The kernel constitutes the foundational commitment to territorial state authority, but readings diverge on whether that authority is unconditional or bounded by human rights obligations.

key_entities: Treaty of Westphalia 1648 (founding document establishing territorial sovereignty)
Sovereign states (rights-holders under absolute reading; duty-bearers under conditional reading)
International intervention advocates (benefit from conditional reading)
Domestic populations under authoritarian rule (victims under absolute reading when rights violated)
United Nations Security Council (enforcement mechanism for conditional reading)
Human rights violating regimes (benefit from absolute reading)
key_tensions: State autonomy vs international accountability (absolute sovereignty vs R2P)
Territorial integrity vs humanitarian intervention (non-interference vs human rights enforcement)

readings.expected_structural_delta: States benefit from non-interference shield; domestic populations under repressive regimes are victims; high ε (0.45-0.60) tangled_rope favoring authoritarian regimes

axiom_contradictions.basis: Accepting sovereignty as unconditional (absolute) requires rejecting that external actors may legitimately override state authority based on internal conduct. Accepting R2P (conditional) requires rejecting that sovereignty shields states from accountability for systematic rights violations. No single framework holds both: either sovereignty is a trump or it isn't.

Absolute sovereignty treats statehood as binary (you have it or you don't); graduated sovereignty treats it as continuous variable. A framework cannot simultaneously hold that sovereignty is unconditional once established AND that sovereignty strength varies with governance quality.

Conditional sovereignty maintains sovereignty's binary character but adds trigger conditions; graduated sovereignty dissolves the binary entirely. The former preserves Westphalian equality-among-sovereigns unless threshold crossed; the latter abandons equality by design. Frameworks holding one must reject the other's foundational structure.

axes.structural_delta: States possess unconditional authority over domestic affairs; external interference categorically illegitimate regardless of internal conduct
axes.primary_observable: State practice in opposing humanitarian interventions; invocations of Article 2(7); vetoes of Security Council resolutions authorizing intervention

axes.selection_reason: Second reading selected: directly contradicts first reading; snare mechanism with moderate ε; essential for kernel contest

axes.structural_delta: Sovereignty strength varies with state capacity and governance legitimacy; creates formal hierarchy among states
axes.primary_observable: Trusteeship arrangements; state-building interventions; differential treatment in international institutions
axes.selection_reason: Third reading selected: introduces structural alternative to binary framework; highest ε; completes triadic kernel decomposition

omegas.description: All three readings face enforcement selectivity: great powers exempt themselves while applying constraints to weaker states. The kernel's authority structure may be downstream of power distribution rather than upstream normative commitment.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + Absence Inventory

omegas.description: European Union has effectively superseded Westphalian sovereignty among members; African Union has distinct sovereignty interpretation (AU Constitutive Act Article 4h). Is this one kernel with regional readings, or multiple kernels?

All readings assume state-centric international order. Transnational corporations, armed non-state actors, and tech platforms exercise authority uncaptured by any reading. Missing axis: post-Westphalian authority distribution.
omegas.source: Absence Inventory (mechanism_count includes no non-state mechanisms)

omegas.description: Westphalia established European state system; global extension occurred via colonialism. Do post-colonial states inherit a kernel designed to exclude them? Authority structure may delegitimize itself for majority of current states.

Drift status marked 'partial' but R2P's 2005 codification vs Westphalia's 1648 origin suggests 357-year interpretive lag followed by rapid norm shift. Is this managed drift or authority structure collapse with replacement?
